thread.title: School spending needs to be curbed
thread.title_full: School spending needs to be curbed

author: ohtadmin
title: School spending needs to be curbed
text:
To the editor:
The sacred cow of Jamestown school spending requires hardnosed critical examination.
The latest school committee proposal argues their nearly $16 million budget represents the lowest increase in 5 years.
Jamestown spends about $30,000 per student (among the highest in the state) compared to Barrington and East Greenwich, which spend about $10,000 less per student yet continue to be the gold standard for Rhode Island academic achievement.
That means Jamestown taxpayers pay about a $4 million premium compared to those two districts to educate the approximately 400 students at Melrose and Lawn schools.
Despite declining student enrollment, Jamestown still operates two schools, employs a superintendent and two principals along with a support staff and assistants.
Declining student enrollment is not going to abate. Jamestown’s student-to-teacher ratio is among the lowest in the state, one-third lower than Barrington and East Greenwich.
The school committee argues our high amount of spending is needed to maintain current levels of student achievement. Most Jamestowners, however, recognize it is our parents who are part of a demographic that values education, holds their children accountable to do the work and who volunteer selflessly that drives high academic achievement, not the schools’ lavish spending.
Jamestown faces serious monetary challenges in the near- and long-term (e.g. funding for the fire department and desperately needed upgrades to water and sewer infrastructure) that will require greater fiscal discipline than either the school committee or the town council have demonstrated the past several years.
At a minimum, the school committee should be required to justify the $4 million premium Jamestown taxpayers are paying.
It also is time the town council require the school committee to submit a serious plan for consolidating students into one building and reducing school administrators as the first steps to get our school budget under control. Both need to start doing a better job of differentiating between want and need rather than continuously asking for more.
Ron Ratcliff
Ship Street
